title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents
claim: Existing monitoring setups either keep observations private or fully public; ours routes an imperfect public signal through the recipient's gossip.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, same node layout, (c) adds a Message node
description: Three side-by-side diagrams share the same layout. A purple Donor circle and a green Recipient circle are joined by a double-headed arrow labeled 'One-shot Game'. A grey 'Non-participants' ellipse sits above them, and a red 'Donor's Action' box sits below. Arrows labeled 'Observed by' run from the action box to the observers. In (a) Private monitoring, only the donor and recipient observe the action, and the non-participants have no incoming arrow. In (b) Perfect public monitoring, an extra long arrow from the action also reaches the non-participants. In (c) Imperfect public monitoring via gossip, the action is observed by the donor and recipient (step 1). The recipient then sends a green 'Message' box a gossip signal (step 2). The message is observed by the donor, the recipient and the non-participants (step 3). Arrows carry numbered labels. Captions (a), (b) and (c) sit below the panels.
caption: Illustration of three monitoring structures: (a) Private monitoring, only the donor and recipient observe the donor's action; (b) Perfect public monitoring, all agents observe the donor's action; (c) Imperfect public monitoring via gossip, only the donor and recipient observe the action, and all agents observe the public signal broadcast by the recipient.
abstract: Indirect reciprocity, which means helping those who have helped others, is difficult to sustain among decentralized, self-interested LLM agents without reliable reputation systems. We address this challenge with the Agentic Linguistic Gossip Network (ALIGN), an automated framework that enables decentralized agents to form reputations, evaluate trustworthiness, and coordinate social norms by strategically sharing open-ended gossip with hierarchical tones. We demonstrate that ALIGN consistently improves indirect reciprocity and resists malicious entrants by identifying and ostracizing defectors. Notably, we find that stronger reasoning capabilities in LLMs lead to more incentive-aligned cooperation, whereas chat models often over-cooperate even when strategically suboptimal. These results suggest that leveraging LLM reasoning through decentralized gossip is a promising path for maintaining social welfare in agentic ecosystems. Our code is available at https://github.com/shuhui-zhu/ALIGN.
